title: First words
goal: Greet people politely or casually, say yes/no, thank, apologise and say goodbye the Marathi way.
intro:
Marathi greetings are simple, but choosing the right level of politeness matters from day one. **नमस्कार** works with anyone; with friends you'll hear काय रे / काय ग and कसा आहेस?

In this unit you'll also meet the three words for 'you' — तू, तुम्ही, आपण — and the basic shape of a Marathi sentence: the verb comes last.

vocab.note: The standard greeting in Maharashtra, with folded hands. Works at any time of day.
Understood everywhere; नमस्कार is more typically Marathi.
The everyday yes. Careful: Hindi हाँ is also heard in Mumbai.
Also negates verbs: मला माहीत नाही 'I don't know'.
Refusing an offer: नको, धन्यवाद. Also 'don't!': नको करू.
Fairly formal; in casual speech people say थँक्यू or just smile.
English loan, extremely common.
मी आभारी आहे 'I am grateful' — formal thanks.
Used on signs and in formal requests. In speech, politeness comes from the verb form (सांगा) and particles like ना, जरा; प्लीज is common too.
Informal: माफ कर.
Mostly in ठीक आहे 'it's OK'.

vocab.en: that works; that's fine (lit. 'it will go')
vocab.note: Very Marathi way to agree to a plan.
n · तुमचं स्वागत आहे 'You are welcome (here)'.
Mostly written or on WhatsApp; in person people just say नमस्कार.
Colloquial: परत parat.
पुन्हा भेटू 'we'll meet again'.
Polite way to get attention; also how a wife traditionally addresses her husband.
Also turns a sentence into a yes/no question at the start: काय, तुम्ही येणार?
f: कशी kashī · n: कसं kasaṃ · m pl / polite: कसे kase · f pl / polite: कशा kashā
f: बरी barī · pl: बरे bare. मी बरा आहे 'I'm well'.
Answer to कसा आहेस?: मजेत!
For friends, children, family members younger than you, and God.
Default for strangers, elders, shopkeepers.
As 'you' it's used in speeches, offices, announcements. In conversation it usually means 'we (you and I)'.
Woman: येते yete. Saying जातो 'I'm going' is avoided as inauspicious.
सावकाश जा 'go carefully' — said to someone leaving.

phrases.en: How are you? (informal, to a man)
phrases.note: To a woman: तू कशी आहेस?

phrases.en: What's up? (lit. 'what do you say?', to a man)
phrases.note: To a woman: काय म्हणतेस? kāy mhaṇtes?

grammar.title: Word order: the verb comes last (SOV)
grammar.body:
A Marathi sentence is normally **Subject – Object – Verb**. Where English says 'I drink tea', Marathi says 'I tea drink': मी चहा पितो.

The verb (or the copula आहे 'is') closes the sentence. Question words usually go just before the verb, and a yes/no question is made by adding **का** at the end.

Word order is flexible for emphasis, but the verb-final pattern is the safe default.

grammar.title: तू, तुम्ही, आपण — three ways to say 'you'
grammar.body:
**तू** (tū) is intimate: friends, younger family, children. Using it with a stranger or elder is rude.

**तुम्ही** (tumhī) is the normal polite 'you' and also the plural. It takes plural verb forms even for one person: तुम्ही कसे आहात?

**आपण** (āpaṇ) is very formal 'you' (speeches, official settings, very senior people). In everyday talk आपण usually means **'we (you and I)'**: आपण जाऊया 'let's go'.

The verb and adjectives agree with the person and gender: तू कसा आहेस (to a man), तू कशी आहेस (to a woman). With तुम्ही, use कसे for men or mixed groups and कशा for women. When unsure, use तुम्ही.

examples.en: How are you? (to a male friend)
How are you? (to a female friend)
How are you? (polite, to a man / group)
How are you? (polite, to a woman)

dialogue.title: Meeting the neighbour
dialogue.setting: Sameer passes his neighbour Mrs Kulkarni (Kaku, 'auntie') on the stairs of their Pune building.

lines.speaker: Sameer
lines.native: मी मजेत आहे. तुम्ही कशा आहात?
lines.roman: mī majet āhe. tumhī kashā āhāt?

lines.speaker: Kaku
lines.native: मी पण बरी आहे. ये ना, चहा घे.
lines.roman: mī paṇ barī āhe. ye nā, tsahā ghe.
lines.en: I'm well too. Come on in, have some tea.

lines.speaker: Sameer
lines.en: No thanks. I'm in a hurry right now.

culture: Marathi speakers rarely say 'goodbye' with a word for 'go'. Instead the person leaving says **येतो / येते** ('I'll come [again]'), and the host replies **या / ये** ('come') or सावकाश जा ('go carefully'). Older neighbours and friends' parents are called **काका** (uncle) and **काकू** (auntie); an elder brother-figure is **दादा** and an elder sister-figure **ताई**. Notice that Kaku calls Sameer **तू** (he's younger) while he calls her **तुम्ही**.
